title: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two last-in-first-out stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue, and analyse the amortised cost.
shortTitle: Implement a Queue Using Two Stacks

s1_definition.profdef: You can build a first-in-first-out queue from two last-in-first-out stacks, an inbox and an outbox. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox. Dequeue takes from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty you first pour the entire inbox into the outbox, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top. Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortised constant time per operation.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture two spikes at the National Bank of India teller window. New customers' request slips go onto the "incoming" spike as they arrive, newest on top. When the teller wants to serve the next customer in fairness order, she checks the "serving" spike; if it is empty she flips the whole incoming pile onto it one by one, which reverses it so the earliest arrival is now on top. She serves from the serving spike until it empties, then flips again only when needed. Each slip gets flipped at most once, so the extra handling averages out to almost nothing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push to an inbox stack, pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty, and each element moves once for amortised constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You can build a first-in-first-out queue from two last-in-first-out stacks, an inbox and an outbox. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox. Dequeue takes from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty you first pour the entire inbox into the outbox, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top. Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortised constant time per operation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture two spikes at the National Bank of India teller window. New customers' request slips go onto the "incoming" spike as they arrive, newest on top. When the teller wants to serve the next customer in fairness order, she checks the "serving" spike; if it is empty she flips the whole incoming pile onto it one by one, which reverses it so the earliest arrival is now on top. She serves from the serving spike until it empties, then flips again only when needed. Each slip gets flipped at most once, so the extra handling averages out to almost nothing.

**One line to remember:** Push to an inbox stack, pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty, and each element moves once for amortised constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
A stack is last-in-first-out and a queue is first-in-first-out, so the trick is to reverse the order using a second stack. The naive approach reverses on every single operation, which is wasteful; the efficient approach reverses lazily, only when the outbox runs dry.

Enqueue is trivial: `inbox.push(x)`. Dequeue is where the design lives. If the outbox is empty, you transfer everything: `while (!inbox.isEmpty()) outbox.push(inbox.pop());`. This single transfer reverses the inbox so the oldest element is now on the top of the outbox. Then you `return outbox.pop();`. If the outbox is not empty, you skip the transfer entirely and just pop the outbox, because it already holds older elements in the right order.

The key insight is the amortised analysis. A single dequeue that triggers a transfer can cost linear time, but each element is pushed to the inbox once, moved to the outbox once, and popped once across its whole lifetime. Spread over all operations, that is a constant number of moves per element, so the amortised cost per operation is constant even though one individual dequeue can be expensive. This distinction between worst-case and amortised cost is exactly what interviewers probe.

A senior-level nuance is when to prefer this over a direct queue. In practice you would use `ArrayDeque` as a real queue; the two-stack construction matters when your only primitive is a stack, for example implementing a queue on top of a persistent or immutable stack in functional code, or demonstrating that queues and stacks are inter-convertible. It also underpins the immutable "Banker's queue" in functional data structures, where two lists stand in for the two stacks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes customer service requests in strict fairness order, oldest first, but the only buffering primitive available in a particular legacy embedded component is a stack. We must present a first-in-first-out queue to the rest of the system while internally using stacks. This is exactly the two-stack queue, because two stacks reverse into the right order.

Problem 2 — Throughput matters, so we cannot afford to reverse the whole buffer on every operation. We need the lazy transfer so that the reversal cost is paid only when the serving side empties, giving amortised constant time per request.

In our mini-project we build a `RequestQueue` backed by two deques used as stacks. The demo enqueues three request IDs, dequeues one, enqueues another, then dequeues the rest, logging the transfer so you can see it happen only when the outbox is empty.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: enqueue request one, two, three, dequeue, enqueue four, then dequeue three times.

Step 1: Enqueue one, two, three. The inbox now holds three on top, then two, then one at the bottom. The outbox is empty.

Step 2: Dequeue. The outbox is empty, so we transfer: pop three and push, pop two and push, pop one and push. Now the outbox holds one on top, then two, then three. We pop the outbox top, request one, the oldest, exactly correct.

Step 3: Enqueue four. It goes onto the inbox. The outbox still holds two on top then three, untouched.

Step 4: Dequeue. The outbox is not empty, so no transfer. Pop the outbox top, request two.

Step 5: Dequeue. The outbox is not empty, pop request three. The outbox is now empty.

Step 6: Dequeue. The outbox is empty, so we transfer the inbox, which currently holds only four. The outbox now holds four on top. Pop it, request four. Every request was served in arrival order, and the only transfers happened when the outbox was empty, confirming amortised constant time.

```
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-1
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-2
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-3
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  enqueue 1,2,3   inbox:[3,2,1]   outbox:[]

  dequeue → outbox empty → transfer
     inbox:[] outbox:[1,2,3]  pop → 1

  enqueue 4       inbox:[4]       outbox:[2,3]
  dequeue → outbox not empty → pop → 2
  dequeue → pop → 3   outbox:[]
  dequeue → transfer inbox:[4]→outbox:[4] → pop → 4
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Queue From Two Stacks ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Two-stack (inbox/outbox) amortisation                        │
  │  Lazy transfer — reverse only when outbox empties             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: RequestQueue only provides FIFO semantics                 │
  │  L: usable anywhere a FIFO buffer is expected                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             RequestQueue              │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - inbox: Deque<String>              │  enqueue side
  │  - outbox: Deque<String>             │  dequeue side
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + enqueue(id): void                  │  O(1)
  │  + dequeue(): String                  │  amortised O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Invariant: FIFO order preserved across both stacks

  ── State Diagram: Dequeue ───────────────────────────────

  [dequeue] ──outbox empty──→ transfer all inbox → outbox
  [dequeue] ──outbox non-empty──→ pop outbox
  [both empty] ──→ throw NoSuchElementException

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. enqueue(id): inbox.push(id)
  2. dequeue(): if outbox empty → pour inbox into outbox
  3.            return outbox.pop()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
You can build a first-in-first-out queue out of two last-in-first-out stacks, which I call the inbox and the outbox. Enqueue is trivial: I just push the new element onto the inbox. Dequeue is where the design lives: I serve from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty I first pour the entire inbox into it, popping from one and pushing to the other, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top of the outbox. Then I pop the outbox.

The important part is doing the transfer lazily, only when the outbox is empty, not on every operation. That gives the amortised analysis its punch. A single dequeue that triggers a transfer can cost linear time, but each element is pushed onto the inbox once, moved to the outbox once, and popped once over its entire lifetime. Spread across all operations, that is a constant number of moves per element, so the amortised cost per operation is constant even though one individual dequeue can be expensive. Explaining that worst-case versus amortised distinction is usually what the interviewer is really checking.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a legacy embedded component whose only buffering primitive was a stack, yet the rest of the system needed strict oldest-first fairness for customer service requests. The two-stack queue let me present proper first-in-first-out semantics while internally using stacks, and the lazy transfer kept throughput high because reversal cost is paid only when the serving side drains.

The senior-level point I make is that in normal Java I would just use ArrayDeque as a real queue; the two-stack construction earns its place when a stack is the only primitive I have, such as implementing a queue over an immutable stack in functional code. It is also the idea behind the Banker's queue in functional data structures, where two lists play the role of the two stacks, so this question is really about understanding that stacks and queues are inter-convertible.
